title: Terrace and Balcony Gardens: What to Check Before You Plant
metaTitle: Terrace & Balcony Gardens: What to Check | Laavin
description: Before a terrace or balcony garden: check structure, waterproofing and drainage, use a lightweight mix and choose plants for Delhi heat.
lead: A terrace garden can cool the floor below, give people a place to sit and turn a hot, empty roof into the best space in the building. It can also leak, overload the slab or die in its first summer. The difference is almost always decided before a single plant goes in.
imageAlt: Young plants growing under a fine irrigation mist
body:
1. Start with the structure

Wet soil is heavy, and a roof slab was usually designed for people and water tanks, not for a garden. Before anything else, have a structural engineer confirm how much load the terrace can safely carry. Plan heavier elements, such as deep planters, trees and water features, over beams and columns rather than in the middle of a span.

2. Fix the waterproofing first

Most terrace garden problems are really waterproofing problems. Inspect the existing membrane, repair or replace it, and add a root barrier so roots cannot work their way into joints. A protection layer over the membrane stops it being punctured during installation.

Then test it. A simple ponding test, where the roof is flooded and checked for leaks over a day or two, is far cheaper than lifting a finished garden to find a leak.

Waterproofing is the one part of a terrace garden you cannot easily redo later. Get it right, and test it, before you plant.

3. Plan the drainage

Water must leave the roof quickly, especially in the monsoon. The usual build-up is a drainage layer over the waterproofing, a filter fabric to keep soil out of it, and then the growing medium. The roof should slope towards outlets, and every outlet should stay reachable for cleaning.

4. Use a lightweight growing mix

Ordinary garden soil is too heavy and compacts in containers. Terrace gardens use a lighter mix, typically built from cocopeat, compost and a mineral such as perlite or vermiculite, which holds water without becoming waterlogged. Depth depends on what you plant: lawns and ground covers need the least, shrubs need more, and small trees need the deepest beds or large planters.

5. Choose plants for heat and wind

A Delhi rooftop is hotter, windier and brighter than the ground below. Plants that cope well include bougainvillea, frangipani, hibiscus, tecoma, ornamental grasses and many succulents. Herbs such as lemongrass and tulsi do well in containers. Keep tall or top-heavy plants away from the edges, and anchor large planters against wind.

  • Full sun and wind: bougainvillea, ornamental grasses, succulents.
  • Flowering colour: hibiscus, tecoma, frangipani in larger planters.
  • Shade and screening: pergolas with climbers rather than heavy trees.

6. Water with drip, on a timer

Rooftop plants dry out fast in May and June and need far less water in winter. A drip system on a timer, with a separate line for any lawn, delivers water at the roots and can be adjusted by season. It also keeps water off the waterproofing where it is not needed.

7. Look after it

Clear every outlet before the monsoon, trim plants that catch the wind, top up the growing mix as it settles, and feed regularly, because containers hold fewer nutrients than open ground.

8. Balconies follow the same rules

A balcony garden is a terrace garden in miniature. Check what the slab can carry, raise planters on feet or trays so water can drain off the floor, use the same lightweight mix, and choose plants for the light the balcony actually gets. Railing planters must be fixed securely, especially on higher floors.

How we approach terrace and balcony gardens

On our team, the structure, waterproofing and drainage are checked by a civil and electrical engineer retired from the Delhi Development Authority, and the plants and growing mix are chosen by a horticulturist with an M.Sc. in Botany. See our landscape services.

proof.text: Structure, waterproofing and drainage checked before planting begins.

title: Planning a Farmhouse Garden for the Delhi NCR Climate
metaTitle: Farmhouse Garden Planning in Delhi NCR | Laavin
description: Planning a farmhouse garden in Delhi NCR: test the soil, plan the water, plant windbreaks and shade, choose a hardy lawn, time it right.
lead: A farmhouse gives you space that a city home never does: room for lawns, an orchard, shade trees and a kitchen garden. It also brings the full force of the NCR climate, from hot dry winds in May to heavy monsoon rain and cold winter nights. A good farmhouse garden is planned around all of it.
imageAlt: Landscaped courtyard with a pergola, lawn and evening lighting
body:
1. Plan the zones before you plant

Walk the plot and divide it into zones: the arrival and driveway, the lawn around the house, an orchard, a kitchen garden, and a service area for water tanks, pumps and storage. Deciding this first stops you planting a tree where a driveway or a pipe needs to go later.

2. Test the soil

Soil across NCR varies a lot, and some areas have alkaline or salty patches that hold plants back. A basic soil test for pH, salinity and organic matter tells you what to correct and which plants will do well. It costs very little compared with replacing plants that never establish.

3. Sort out the water

Know where your water comes from, how much you have and how good it is. Check the local rules on groundwater use, and plan rainwater harvesting so that monsoon water recharges the ground instead of running off. Lay out the main pipelines before planting, so you are not digging up a new lawn later.

On a farmhouse, water decides almost everything else. Plan it first, and the garden becomes far easier to keep alive.

4. Plant windbreaks and shade trees early

Trees take the longest to grow, so plant them first. A row of trees along the boundary that faces the hot summer winds protects everything inside it. Native and naturalised trees such as neem, arjun, jamun and pilkhan cope with the heat, give dense shade and need little care once established.

5. Choose a lawn that can take the heat

Doob grass, a Bermuda type, handles north Indian summers and heavy use well. Keep large lawns where you will actually use them, and use ground covers or mulched beds in the rest. That saves a great deal of water and mowing.

6. Add an orchard and kitchen garden

Mango, guava, citrus, pomegranate, amla and jamun all grow well in the region. Plant them in well-prepared pits with compost, protect young trees from animals, and give each one enough room to reach full size. A small kitchen garden near the house, with raised beds and drip lines, keeps fresh herbs and vegetables within easy reach.

7. Time planting with the seasons

  • Monsoon, July to September: the best time for most trees and shrubs.
  • February and March: a good second window before the heat.
  • May and June: avoid new planting; focus on watering what is already in the ground.

8. Water with drip and sprinklers

Use drip lines for trees, beds and the orchard, and sprinklers only for the lawn. Split the system into zones by water need and run it on timers, so each area gets what it needs without waste.

How we approach farmhouse gardens

Our horticulturist, who holds an M.Sc. in Botany and has 30+ years of field experience, chooses species for your soil and the season, and the same team designs and installs the irrigation. See our landscape services and irrigation services.

title: Landscaping for Hotels and Resorts: A Practical Guide
metaTitle: Hotel & Resort Landscaping Guide | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Landscaping a hotel or resort: plan the guest journey, plant arrival courts and pool decks, build event lawns that recover, and upkeep.
lead: In a hotel, the landscape is part of the product. Guests judge the property by the arrival court before they reach the lobby, photograph the pool deck and remember the lawn where the wedding was held. Unlike most landscapes, it has to look its best every single day.
imageAlt: Courtyard with a water channel, palms and flowering trees
body:
1. Design around the guest journey

Follow the path a guest takes: the gate, the driveway, the arrival court, the lobby, the rooms, the pool, the restaurants and the event spaces. Each stop needs a different kind of landscape, and the moments guests notice most deserve the most care.

2. Make the arrival court count

The arrival court sets the first impression. Use bold, simple planting that reads well from a moving car, a focal point such as a tree, sculpture or water feature, and lighting that makes it just as striking at night. Choose plants that stay tidy all year rather than ones that look spectacular for a few weeks.

3. Plant pool decks with care

Around pools, avoid thorny plants and trees that drop heavy leaves, fruit or flowers into the water. Give loungers real shade, keep roots well away from the pool shell and paving, and use planting to screen service areas and neighbouring buildings.

A hotel landscape is judged on its worst day, not its best. Choose plants and layouts that stay neat with routine care.

4. Build event lawns that recover

Wedding and event lawns take heavy footfall, stages and marquees. They need a hard-wearing grass, good sub-surface drainage so they dry quickly after rain, and a maintenance plan that includes rest, aeration and repair between events.

5. Bring green indoors and onto terraces

Green walls and large planters soften lobbies, corridors and restaurant terraces. They need built-in irrigation, the right light, and plants chosen for indoor or partly shaded conditions.

6. Light it for the evening

Many guests see the grounds mostly after dark. Warm uplighting on trees, low path lights and underwater lights in water features extend the landscape into the evening and make the property feel safe and welcoming.

7. Water efficiently

Drip irrigation for beds and planters and zoned sprinklers for lawns keep water use under control. Where treated water from the property is available for irrigation, check its quality before using it on sensitive plants.

8. Maintain without disturbing guests

  • Schedule mowing, pruning and spraying for early mornings or low-occupancy days.
  • Use quieter equipment near rooms and dining areas.
  • Plan seasonal colour changes ahead of peak periods and major events.

How we approach hotel grounds

One team designs the planting, irrigation, hardscape and lighting and then maintains them, so nothing falls between contractors. Water features and lighting are overseen by our engineer, who spent 30+ years with the Delhi Development Authority. See our landscape services and hardscaping services.

cta.text: Share the property location, a site plan or a few photos, and the spaces you want to improve. We will reply within 24 hours with ideas and an estimate.

title: Vertical Gardens and Green Walls: How to Keep Them Alive
metaTitle: Vertical Gardens & Green Walls Guide | Laavin
description: How vertical gardens work: choosing a system, protecting the wall, irrigation and light, plants for indoor and outdoor walls, and upkeep.
lead: A green wall can turn a bare facade, a lobby or a boundary wall into the most memorable part of a building. It is also one of the easiest landscapes to get wrong. A vertical garden has very little soil and no room for error, so it lives or dies by its system, its water and its light.
imageAlt: Lush trailing plants and greenery in a bright room
body:
1. Choose the right system

There are a few common ways to build a vertical garden, and each suits a different site and budget:

  • Modular panels or trays: plants grow in pre-planted units that clip onto a frame. Easy to replace one section at a time.
  • Felt or pocket systems: plants sit in fabric pockets fixed to a waterproof backing. Light and flexible, but they need very reliable watering.
  • Green facades: climbers grow up wires or a trellis from planters at the base. The simplest and lowest-maintenance option for large outdoor walls, though slower to fill in.

2. Protect the wall behind it

A green wall keeps a lot of moisture against a building. The system should stand slightly off the wall on a frame, with a waterproof backing between the plants and the structure, so water never soaks into plaster or brickwork. The frame and fixings need to carry the full wet weight of the panels.

3. Irrigation is not optional

With so little growing medium, a vertical garden dries out within days if watering fails. It needs drip irrigation on a timer, emitters spread so every part of the wall gets water, and a gutter or tray at the base to catch the runoff. On larger walls, splitting the system into zones helps, because the top dries faster than the bottom.

Most failed green walls die of water problems: a blocked emitter, a timer that stopped, or a dry patch nobody noticed. Plan the irrigation as carefully as the planting.

4. Match the plants to the light

Light decides which plants will survive. Outdoor walls in full Delhi sun need hardy, heat-tolerant species, while shaded walls can take ferns and foliage plants. Indoors, most walls are darker than they look, so choose plants that tolerate low light, such as money plant, philodendron, syngonium and peace lily, or add grow lights where daylight is weak.

5. Think about the weather

Outdoor walls face hot dry winds in May and June and heavy rain in the monsoon. Plan for more frequent watering in summer, check that drainage copes with downpours, and avoid placing tender plants on the most exposed sides.

6. Plan the upkeep

  • Trim plants regularly so the wall stays even and nothing smothers its neighbours.
  • Check emitters and the timer often, and clean filters so lines do not clog.
  • Feed through the irrigation or by hand, because the medium holds few nutrients.
  • Replace weak plants quickly, before gaps spread.

How we approach vertical gardens

Our engineer checks the wall, the frame and the waterproofing, our horticulturist chooses plants for the light and exposure, and the same team installs and maintains the drip irrigation. See our landscape services.

title: Balcony Gardens: A Practical Guide for Apartments
metaTitle: Balcony Gardens for Apartments | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Planning an apartment balcony garden: read the light, respect weight and drainage, pick containers and plants, and water simply.
lead: A balcony is often the only outdoor space an apartment has, and a few well-chosen plants can make it the favourite spot in the home. Balconies are small, exposed and shared with neighbours below, so a good balcony garden is planned around light, weight and water from the start.
imageAlt: Potting soil, a trowel and young plants ready for containers
body:
1. Read the light first

The direction a balcony faces decides what will grow. An east-facing balcony gets gentle morning sun, a north-facing one stays bright but mostly shaded, and south and west faces get strong afternoon heat in a Delhi summer. Watch your balcony for a day and note how many hours of direct sun it gets before choosing plants.

2. Respect the weight and the floor

Wet soil and large pots are heavier than they look. Keep the heaviest containers near the wall or the edge supported by the building, not in the middle of a cantilevered slab. Raise pots on feet or trays so water can drain and the balcony floor stays dry, and check your society's rules before fixing anything to walls or railings.

3. Make sure water drains the right way

Water dripping onto the balcony below is the fastest way to upset a neighbour. Use pots with drainage holes, sit them in saucers or trays, and make sure the balcony floor drains to its outlet rather than over the edge.

On a balcony, the best garden is one your neighbours never notice: no drips, no falling pots, no leaves blowing onto the floor below.

4. Pick the right containers

Lighter containers, such as good-quality plastic, fibreglass or lightweight composite, keep the load down. Fill them with a light potting mix rather than garden soil. Railing planters should be fixed securely, especially on higher floors where the wind is stronger.

5. Choose plants for your light

  • Full sun: bougainvillea, hibiscus, succulents, and herbs such as tulsi and lemongrass.
  • Part sun: money plant, spider plant, syngonium and many flowering annuals in winter.
  • Shade: ferns, peace lily and other foliage plants that prefer softer light.

6. Keep watering simple

Small pots dry out quickly in summer and need far less water in winter. A small drip kit on a timer, or self-watering pots, keeps plants healthy when you travel and stops the overwatering that rots roots.

7. Plan for wind and birds

Higher floors catch more wind, so choose sturdy, low plants for exposed balconies and avoid tall pots near the railing. Pigeons are a common problem in many apartment blocks; bird netting keeps the garden and the floor clean.

How we approach balcony gardens

We check the weight, drainage and fixings, choose plants for the light your balcony actually gets, and can install a compact drip system so the garden looks after itself. See our landscape services.

title: How Mature Trees Are Transplanted on Highway Projects
metaTitle: How Mature Trees Are Transplanted on Highways | Laavin
description: How mature trees are moved out of road-widening corridors and kept alive: species, timing, root-ball preparation, replanting and aftercare.
lead: Highway widening and new infrastructure often run straight through rows of mature trees. Felling them is quick, but it costs the city decades of shade and canopy, and it increasingly costs the project time in approvals and public objection. Transplantation lets the corridor be cleared while the trees live on nearby. Here is how it works in practice, and what decides whether a moved tree survives.
imageAlt: Mature tree being lifted by crane for transplantation
body:
1. Survey: which trees can be moved

Not every tree is a good candidate. The survey records each tree's species, girth, health and access for machinery. Fig species such as peepal, banyan and pilkhan generally recover well from transplantation. Trees with a deep taproot, or that are already diseased, hollow or leaning, are harder to move successfully. The survey also checks where the trees will go: the receiving site needs space, workable soil and a water source.

2. Timing and preparation

In north India, the monsoon months are usually the best window, because humidity is high and the tree loses less water while its roots recover. Peak summer is the worst. Preparation starts weeks before the move: the tree is watered deeply, the canopy is pruned back so there is less leaf to support, and roots around the future root ball are cut in stages to encourage new feeder roots inside it.

3. Digging, wrapping and lifting

The root ball is sized to the trunk: the bigger the tree, the larger and heavier the ball. It is dug out carefully, wrapped in hessian and secured so the soil stays tight around the roots. Cranes and earth-movers lift the tree onto a trailer. The goal throughout is to keep the root ball intact and the time out of the ground as short as possible, ideally replanting the same day.

Plan transplantation into the construction schedule early. Survey and root preparation take weeks, and the best season may not match your earthwork dates.

4. Replanting

The receiving pit is dug wider than the root ball, with good drainage and improved soil. The tree goes in at the same depth and, where possible, facing the same direction as before. It is then braced with guy wires or stakes so wind cannot rock it while new roots anchor it.

5. Aftercare decides survival

Most of the work happens after the move. For the first year the tree needs regular watering, rooting treatments, protection against fungal infection and pests, and inspections. New leaf growth is the first sign it has taken. Survival is a contractual issue as well as an environmental one: Delhi's 2020 tree transplantation policy, for example, requires that at least 80% of transplanted trees survive.

In practice: NH-307

On the NH-307 widening, Laavin Infrascapes relocated 155 mature roadside trees for an NHAI project, working through the process above alongside the road contractor's schedule.

title: Carbon Sequestration Through Avenue and Median Plantation
metaTitle: Carbon Sequestration by Avenue Plantation | Laavin
description: How avenue and median plantation sequesters carbon, how to estimate it, which species suit north India, and why survival matters most.
lead: Every highway project in India now carries a green component. Under the Green Highways Policy 2015, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways set aside 1% of highway project costs for plantation and its upkeep. Done well, avenue trees and median planting become one of the few parts of a road that actively take carbon out of the air. Done badly, they die within two summers and store almost nothing.
imageAlt: Flowering shrubs on a highway median with avenue trees along the road
body:
How trees store carbon

Trees take in carbon dioxide as they grow and lock the carbon into wood, roots and leaves. Roughly half of a tree's dry weight is carbon, and every tonne of stored carbon equals about 3.67 tonnes of CO₂ removed from the atmosphere, the ratio of their molecular weights. So the carbon a plantation stores depends mainly on how much wood it grows. That depends on species, growth rate and lifespan, and above all on whether the plants survive.

Avenue trees and median shrubs do different jobs

Avenue plantation, the rows of trees along the edges of a road, does most of the carbon work. A large, long-lived tree keeps adding wood for decades. Medians are different. They are usually planted with shrubs kept low enough to block headlight glare without hiding traffic, so their woody biomass stays small. Medians still matter, but mainly for other reasons.

  • Avenue rows: large, long-lived trees. The highest carbon storage, plus shade for pedestrians and cyclists.
  • Medians: dense, low shrubs. Modest carbon storage; the main benefits are glare reduction, dust capture and appearance.
  • Green belts beyond the road edge: multi-row planting where land allows, combining tall trees and shrubs for both carbon and screening.

Species that work in north India

For avenue rows, native and naturalised trees that tolerate heat, dust and dry spells perform best. Neem, peepal, pilkhan, arjun, jamun, amaltas and kachnar are common choices. Fig species such as peepal and pilkhan grow large and live long, which makes them strong carbon stores. For medians, hardy shrubs such as kaner (oleander) and bougainvillea are widely used because they cope with pollution, heat and limited watering.

Mix species rather than planting one along an entire stretch, so a single pest or disease can't wipe out the plantation. Spacing and setbacks follow the project specifications and road safety rules: trees must not block sight lines at junctions or crowd utilities.

Estimating the carbon a plantation stores

Credible estimates come from measurements, not per-tree rules of thumb. The usual method is:

  1. Measure each tree's trunk diameter at breast height (1.3 m) and, ideally, its height.
  2. Apply a published allometric equation for the species or forest type to estimate above-ground dry biomass.
  3. Add below-ground (root) biomass, usually estimated as a fraction of the above-ground figure.
  4. Multiply total dry biomass by the carbon fraction (about 0.47, the IPCC default) to get stored carbon.
  5. Multiply the carbon by 3.67 to express it as CO₂.

Repeat the measurements every year or two, and the difference is the carbon sequestered over that period. Treat headline "kilograms per tree per year" figures with caution: young roadside trees store very little in their first years, and real values vary widely by species and site.

A dead sapling stores no carbon. On most roadside plantations, survival matters more than the number of saplings planted.

What decides survival

Roadside plants face heat, dust, vehicle damage, grazing animals and irregular watering. The plantations that survive have a few things in common:

  • Larger, nursery-hardened saplings rather than small seedlings.
  • Tree guards against animals and vehicles.
  • Reliable watering through the first two to three summers, ideally drip lines along medians and avenue rows.
  • Prompt replacement of failed plants, written into the maintenance contract.
  • Mature tree transplantation instead of felling when a road is widened. An existing large tree already holds decades of stored carbon that a new sapling would take decades to replace.

Carbon credits and green credits

Plantation projects can earn carbon credits under international standards such as Verra's Verified Carbon Standard or Gold Standard. Credits require baseline studies, long-term monitoring and third-party verification, so they are usually practical only for large or aggregated projects. In India, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change launched the Green Credit Programme in 2023, and tree plantation is one of the activities it covers. If credits are part of the plan, design the monitoring from day one.

From our work

We planted 3,500 hardy, pollution-tolerant plants on the NH-7 median for an NHAI contractor. On NH-307 we relocated 155 mature trees instead of felling them during road widening. See our plantation and transplantation services.

title: Landscaping for Office Premises: A Practical Guide
metaTitle: Office Landscaping: A Practical Guide | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Landscaping office premises in India: shade, plant choice, water-efficient irrigation, terrace gardens, green building credits and upkeep.
lead: An office's landscape is the first thing visitors see and one of the few parts of the building people choose to spend time in. It also costs money every month to water and maintain. Good office landscaping balances the two: spaces people actually use, built from plants and systems that are affordable to keep alive.
imageAlt: Office courtyard with water channel, seating and palms
body:
Start with how people use the site

Walk the site with the facility team and map how people move and where they stop: the entrance and drop-off, walkways between buildings, parking, break and smoking areas, places people take calls or eat lunch, and the views from desks and meeting rooms. Put the best landscaping where people are. Low-traffic edges and service areas can stay simple and cheap to maintain.

Shade comes first

In an Indian summer, shade is the most valued feature of any outdoor space. Plant shade trees over parking, along walkways and around seating. Where trees will take years to grow, pergolas and shade structures fill the gap.

Choose plants for the site, not the brochure

  • Favour native and well-adapted species. They need less water, fewer chemicals and less replacement.
  • Group plants by water need so thirsty and drought-tolerant plants aren't on the same watering schedule.
  • Keep lawns where people use them. Lawns are the thirstiest part of a landscape; use ground covers and shrub beds elsewhere.
  • Plan for the full-grown size so trees don't crowd buildings, block signage or lift paving in five years.

Water: the biggest running cost

Use drip irrigation for shrub beds, hedges and trees, and sprinklers on timers for lawns. If the campus has a sewage treatment plant, treated water can often be used for irrigation with proper filtration. Rainwater harvesting and recharge pits reduce runoff and top up groundwater. Our guide to drip irrigation for large campuses covers where each system pays off.

Terrace gardens and green walls

Terrace gardens turn unused roofs into breakout space and help insulate the floor below. They need proper waterproofing, a root barrier, a drainage layer and lightweight soil, and your structural engineer should confirm the roof can carry the load before design starts. Green walls look striking in lobbies and on facades, but they depend on built-in irrigation and regular care, so budget for maintenance from the start.

Green building ratings

Landscaping can contribute to green building ratings such as IGBC and GRIHA through native planting, limited lawn area, efficient irrigation and shade that reduces the heat island effect. If your building is pursuing a rating, bring the landscape contractor in early so the design supports the credits you are targeting.

A design your team can't maintain will start declining within a year. Agree the maintenance scope at the design stage, not after handover.

Maintenance is where landscapes succeed or fail

Every landscape needs scheduled pruning, mowing, fertilising, pest control and irrigation checks. Agree who does what, how often, and how plant failures are replaced. A simple monthly report with photographs keeps everyone honest.

Checklist for facility managers

  • Site plan and photographs of the current condition.
  • Where people walk, park, sit and gather.
  • Water source and quality: municipal supply, borewell or treated STP water.
  • Roof loads and waterproofing status, if terraces are in scope.
  • Green building rating targets, if any.
  • Budget for both construction and the first year of maintenance.

See our campus and commercial landscaping services.

title: Industrial Green Belts: Meeting Environmental Clearance Conditions
metaTitle: Industrial Green Belts and EC Conditions | Laavin
description: Planning an industrial green belt that meets environmental clearance conditions: area, density, species, fuel-site safety and records.
lead: Most industries that need an environmental clearance, or consent from a state pollution control board, find a green belt condition attached: a band of dense planting around the site to trap dust, buffer noise and screen the plant from neighbours. Inspectors check it. A green belt that exists on paper but not on the ground can become a compliance problem.
imageAlt: Saplings growing in a nursery under misting irrigation
body:
What the conditions usually ask for

Conditions are specific to each project, so start by reading your own clearance and consent orders. Requirements that appear frequently include:

  • A green belt covering around a third (33%) of the plot area.
  • Planting density of around 2,500 trees per hectare.
  • Native species, planted in multiple rows along the boundary.
  • Survival records and periodic compliance reports.

Designing the belt

Effective green belts are layered. Tall trees go on the outer rows, medium trees in the middle and dense shrubs on the inside, creating a continuous screen from ground level to canopy. Put the densest planting between the main emission sources and the nearest neighbours, taking the prevailing wind direction into account. Leave access routes for fire tenders, maintenance vehicles and inspections.

Choosing species

Pick species that tolerate dust and pollution, stay green through the year and have leaves that hold dust well; rough or hairy leaf surfaces trap more particles. Neem, peepal, arjun, jamun and false ashoka are common choices in north India, and bamboo can create a quick screen while slower trees establish. Mixing species protects the belt from a single pest or disease.

Safety-sensitive sites

At fuel facilities, chemical plants and other hazardous sites, safety norms restrict what can be planted near storage tanks, pipelines and process areas. The green belt has to respect clear zones, avoid build-up of dry leaf litter and keep firebreaks open. Work with the site safety team from the start, and plan the belt around the hazardous-area layout rather than the other way round.

At the Delhi Airport fuel facility, we built a green belt and landscape designed around the site's safety requirements.

Getting trees to survive on industrial land

Industrial plots often have compacted, filled or poor soil. Survival depends on preparing generous pits with good soil and compost, reliable irrigation (treated effluent can sometimes be used if quality and permissions allow), protection from vehicles and animals, and prompt replacement of failures. Plan maintenance for at least the first three years; that is when most losses happen.

Keep records for compliance

Maintain a planting map, a species-wise inventory, survival counts, dated photographs and maintenance logs. Good records make compliance reporting quick and give you evidence if the green belt is questioned during an inspection.

title: Building a School Cricket Ground That Drains After Rain
metaTitle: Building a Cricket Ground That Drains | Laavin
description: Building a school cricket ground that drains after rain: levelling, sub-surface drainage, Bermuda outfields, the pitch square and upkeep.
lead: A school ground takes more punishment than almost any other turf: daily PE classes, inter-house matches, sports days and events, with the monsoon on top. The difference between a ground that is playable the morning after rain and one that stays waterlogged for days is mostly underground.
imageAlt: Large maintained lawn on a landscaped campus
body:
1. Survey and levels

Start with a topographic survey of the ground. The design gives the surface a gentle, even fall so water runs off instead of pooling, while staying flat enough for fair play. Precise grading with laser-guided equipment produces a far more even surface than levelling by eye.

2. Sub-surface drainage

Surface fall alone can't clear heavy monsoon rain. A sub-surface drainage system uses perforated pipes laid in gravel-filled trenches, usually in a herringbone pattern, leading to an outfall or a rainwater harvesting pit. On heavy clay soils, narrow sand-filled slits across the surface help water reach the drains faster.

3. Root zone and outfield turf

The outfield turf grows in a sandy root zone laid over the drainage layer, which lets water pass through quickly. Bermuda grass, known locally as doob, is the most widely used warm-season turf in India: it handles heat and heavy wear and recovers quickly. It can be established from sprigs or laid as turf, and needs a grow-in period of several weeks to a few months before the ground can take full use.

4. The pitch square

The pitch is built separately from the outfield, using clay-rich soil compacted in layers so it plays firm and true. It needs regular rolling, mowing and preparation before matches. Practice nets with synthetic pitches take daily wear away from the main square.

5. Running track

A track around the ground needs a compacted base, edging and its own drainage. The surface choice, such as murram or cinder versus synthetic, decides both the cost and how much upkeep the track needs.

Schedule construction so the grow-in finishes before the academic session starts. A ground opened too early gets damaged before the turf has rooted.

6. Irrigation and maintenance

Sprinklers or pop-up irrigation keep the outfield even through dry months. A maintenance calendar should cover mowing, aeration, top dressing, fertilising, weed control and rest periods after heavy use. Training the school's ground staff is part of the job.

From our work

For Angels Public School, Faridabad, we built a cricket ground, a multi-lane running track and sub-surface drainage. See our sports turf and grounds services.

title: Drip Irrigation for Large Campuses: Where It Pays Off
metaTitle: Drip Irrigation for Large Campuses | Laavin Infrascapes
description: Where drip irrigation pays off on large campuses and highway plantations, how to zone and automate it, using STP water, and maintenance.
lead: Watering is one of the largest running costs of a big landscape, and on many Indian campuses it is still done with hoses and flooding. Drip and automated irrigation can cut that cost substantially, but only when the right system goes to the right part of the site.
imageAlt: Plant nursery with misting irrigation system
body:
How drip irrigation works

Drip systems deliver water slowly through emitters placed at each plant's roots, so very little is lost to evaporation or runoff. Drip is commonly cited at around 90% water-use efficiency, compared with roughly half that for flood or hose watering. It also keeps foliage and paths dry, which reduces disease and weeds.

Where drip pays off

  • Shrub beds, hedges and ground covers.
  • Trees, including avenue rows and median plantations along roads.
  • Terrace gardens, planters and green walls.

Where it doesn't

Lawns and sports turf need even coverage across the whole surface, so sprinklers or pop-up heads on timers work better there. Most large campuses end up with a mix: drip for planting beds and trees, sprinklers for turf.

Zoning: the step most systems skip

Group plants with similar water needs, sun exposure and soil into zones, each with its own valve and schedule. A shaded shrub bed and a sunny lawn should never share a schedule. Good zoning is what turns an irrigation system from a convenience into a real water saving.

Automation

Controllers run each zone on its own schedule, at times of day when evaporation is lowest. Rain or soil-moisture sensors can skip a cycle after rain. Larger systems can be monitored and adjusted remotely, which helps when the grounds team is small.

Water sources and filtration

Municipal supply, borewells and treated sewage (STP) water can all feed a drip system. Treated water saves fresh water but carries particles and nutrients that clog emitters, so it needs good filtration and regular flushing. Hard borewell water can leave scale in emitters and may need periodic treatment.

Most drip systems fail through neglect, not design. Budget for filter cleaning, line flushing and emitter checks from the first month.

Maintenance

Clean filters regularly, flush lateral lines, check emitters for clogging, repair damage from mowing or digging, and adjust schedules as the seasons change. A system that is looked after will keep saving water for years.

What we need to design your system

  • Site and planting plan.
  • Water source, available pressure and water quality.
  • Details of any existing irrigation that could be reused.

See our irrigation services, and our guide to office landscaping for how irrigation fits into the wider design.
